checks: Compactness gives finitely many nonempty lattice fibers. Each is compact convex, so its Hausdorff dimension is its affine dimension, and the maximum of those dimensions is q by the finite union formula. The fibers of dimension q have positive finite q-measure. Lower-dimensional fibers are q-null.

If an integral base is a convex combination of positive bases, fix one point in each contributing fiber except the first. The homothetic translated copy of the first fiber in the target fiber has q-measure scaled by the positive factor lambda_1^q. This establishes intrinsic lattice-convexity without any common-direction assumption, including q<d and rank-deficient base support.

The diagonal array meets both constraints. Nonnegativity and the column equalities bound each entry by the corresponding positive weight, and all constraints are closed. The feasible set is compact, so its linear objective attains a minimum. The positive rows form a nonempty set because the column sums have positive total.

The stated epsilon keeps every donor entry nonnegative. The subrow mass and first moment are respectively epsilon*lambda_a and epsilon*lambda_a*j_a. Their sum has mass epsilon and first moment epsilon*j. Row moment residuals and column sums are preserved by linearity, including if the receiver is also a donor or was initially empty.

Expanding each squared displacement and using sum(lambda_a)=1 and sum(lambda_a*j_a)=j verifies the exact objective decrease. It is strictly positive because the donor indices are distinct and have positive coefficients. A lattice point outside V but in its hull, or a member of V that is not a vertex, would give one of the forbidden representations. The parity midpoint argument gives at most 2^n targets, including the singleton case.

The retained row weights and first moments match the companion theorem after dropping zero rows. Its conclusion supplies ambient convex winner cells with at most k-1 cuts, dimension q, pairwise mixed-null overlaps and full ambient coverage. Taking the base of the centroid yields j, and convexity gives membership in that cell. Finite coverage with pairwise null overlaps gives the displayed sum of masses.

For a full-dimensional compact convex K the product with the unit n-cube is an ambient convex body, has q=d, and has exactly the 2^n positive binary fibers. Each integral-mean class has all coordinates in [0,1] with integer expectations. Each zero or one expectation forces that coordinate almost surely, so even arbitrary fractional densities summing to one must give every positive vertex its own class.

overlap.comparison: Its accepted statement gives the empty lattice centroid hull and a stronger affine-rank count for globally extendable tables. Its proof through the count uses only completeness and positive weights, and uses exactly this arbitrary convex-combination merge after normalization by total weight. Its affine equality cells describe row supports on the base. Shared winning bases can carry positive mass in several rows, so these cells alone do not realize their weights as disjoint mixed pieces.

Proof (17) and the following paragraphs give the same quadratic program and midpoint move for complete positive d-volume fiber weights. The fractional 2^n count is already present there. Its geometric results concern mixtures at a target fiber, with no exhaustive winner partition of the original body.

Its globally extendable-table result replaces the quadratic objective by a general strictly convex cost and again proves the vertex/lattice-hull conclusion for fractional rows. It does not simultaneously realize the rows as convex subsets of the original mixed body.

Its full d-volume theorem realizes one selected mass and integral base mean by a convex cap, with a directional centroid comparison. For two feasible labels the complementary cap inherits the remaining moments by subtraction, because the cut is mixed-null. This does not realize simultaneous prescribed moments for arbitrary k or intrinsic q<d.
